description: Symbolic and numeric calculus in the Wolfram Language: differentiation and integration, limits and series expansions, sums and products, ordinary and partial differential equations, vector calculus operators, and the integral transforms used in analysis and signal work. Most functions come in an exact symbolic version and an N-prefixed numeric counterpart.

tools.name: D
tools.description: Computes partial derivatives symbolically. D[f, x] differentiates once with respect to x, D[f, {x, n}] takes the n-th derivative, and several variable specifications give mixed partials. D[f, {vars}] with a list produces the gradient vector, and the NonConstants option marks symbols that implicitly depend on the differentiation variable.
tools.usage:
D[f, x]
D[f, {x, n}]
D[f, x, y]
D[f, {{x, y}}]
D[f, x, NonConstants -> {y}]
tools.notes: D treats other symbols as constants; Dt takes total derivatives and assumes nothing. For a derivative evaluated at a point, use Derivative or D[...] /. x -> value.

tools.name: Derivative
tools.description: Represents the derivative of a function as a function itself, written f' for the first derivative and f'' or Derivative[2][f] for higher orders. Because the result is a function, it can be applied at a point directly, which is what you need for Newton iterations and boundary conditions. Derivative[n1, n2][f] gives mixed partials of a multivariate function.
tools.usage:
f'[x]
f''[x]
Derivative[n][f]
Derivative[n1, n2][f][x, y]
tools.example:
f[x_] := x^3;
f'[2]
Derivative[2][Sin][0]
D[g[x], x] /. x -> 1
Derivative[1, 0][h][x, y]
tools.notes: f'[2] differentiates then evaluates at 2, whereas D[f[2], x] is zero because f[2] is a constant. Use Derivative or a held expression when a derivative at a point is needed.

tools.name: Dt
tools.description: Computes total derivatives, assuming that every symbol may depend on the differentiation variable unless declared constant. Dt[f] with no variable gives the total differential in terms of Dt[x] symbols. Use the Constants option, or set Constant as an attribute, to mark quantities that do not vary.
tools.usage:
Dt[f]
Dt[f, x]
Dt[f, x, Constants -> {c}]
tools.example:
Dt[x^2 + y^2, x]
Dt[x y]
Dt[a x^2, x, Constants -> {a}]
Solve[Dt[x^2 + y^2 == 1, x], Dt[y, x]]
tools.notes: Dt is the right tool for implicit differentiation; D assumes independence and would give a different answer.

tools.name: Integrate
tools.description: Computes indefinite and definite integrals symbolically, including multiple integrals with iterated ranges and integrals over geometric regions. Definite integrals may include parameters, in which case Assumptions constrains them so a closed form exists. The result of an indefinite integral omits the constant of integration and may be valid only on parts of the domain.
tools.usage:
Integrate[f, x]
Integrate[f, {x, a, b}]
Integrate[f, {x, a, b}, {y, c, d}]
Integrate[f, {x, y} \[Element] reg]
Integrate[f, {x, a, b}, Assumptions -> assum]

parameters.name: Assumptions
parameters.description: Conditions on parameters that make the integral convergent or single-valued.

parameters.name: PrincipalValue
parameters.description: Set to True to compute a Cauchy principal value for an integral with a pole on the path.

parameters.name: GenerateConditions
parameters.description: Whether to return ConditionalExpression results describing when the answer is valid.

tools.example:
Integrate[x^2, x]
Integrate[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}]
Integrate[Exp[-a x^2], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}, Assumptions -> a > 0]
Integrate[x y, {x, 0, 1}, {y, 0, x}]
Integrate[1/x, {x, -1, 1}, PrincipalValue -> True]
tools.notes: Iterated ranges are given outermost first, with inner limits allowed to depend on outer variables. If Integrate returns unevaluated, try Assumptions, a substitution, or NIntegrate for a numeric answer.

tools.name: NIntegrate
tools.description: Computes definite integrals numerically using adaptive quadrature, supporting multidimensional integrals, oscillatory integrands, singularities and infinite ranges. Intermediate points listed in the range specification tell it where to split the domain at known singularities or discontinuities. The Method option selects from a large library of strategies and rules.
tools.usage:
NIntegrate[f, {x, a, b}]
NIntegrate[f, {x, a, c, b}]
NIntegrate[f, {x, a, b}, {y, c, d}]
NIntegrate[f, {x, a, b}, Method -> m, WorkingPrecision -> p]

parameters.name: WorkingPrecision
parameters.description: Precision used internally; raise it together with PrecisionGoal for high-accuracy results.

parameters.name: MaxRecursion
parameters.description: Maximum subdivision depth for adaptive strategies.

tools.example:
NIntegrate[Sin[x]/x, {x, 0, Infinity}]
NIntegrate[Exp[-x^2], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}]
NIntegrate[1/Sqrt[x], {x, 0, 1}]
NIntegrate[f[x, y], {x, 0, 1}, {y, 0, 1}, Method -> "MonteCarlo"]
NIntegrate[Sin[1/x], {x, 0, 1}, MaxRecursion -> 20]
tools.notes: Define integrands with the _?NumericQ pattern so NIntegrate never tries to evaluate them symbolically. For high dimensions use "MonteCarlo" or "QuasiMonteCarlo" rather than adaptive subdivision.

tools.name: Limit
tools.description: Computes the limit of an expression as a variable approaches a value, including limits at infinity and one-sided limits via the Direction option. It handles indeterminate forms, essential singularities and limits involving parameters, returning Indeterminate or an interval when no single limit exists. Multi-variable limits can be taken with a list of variable rules.
tools.usage:
Limit[expr, x -> a]
Limit[expr, x -> a, Direction -> "FromAbove"]
Limit[expr, {x -> a, y -> b}]
Limit[expr, x -> Infinity]

parameters.name: Direction
parameters.description: "FromAbove"/-1 for the right-hand limit, "FromBelow"/1 for the left-hand limit, or Reals for a two-sided limit.

parameters.name: Assumptions
parameters.description: Conditions on parameters appearing in the expression.

tools.example:
Limit[Sin[x]/x, x -> 0]
Limit[(1 + 1/n)^n, n -> Infinity]
Limit[1/x, x -> 0, Direction -> "FromAbove"]
Limit[Abs[x]/x, x -> 0]
Limit[x^n, x -> Infinity, Assumptions -> n > 0]
tools.notes: MaxLimit and MinLimit give the limit superior and inferior when the limit does not exist; DiscreteLimit handles limits of sequences over integers.

tools.name: Series
tools.description: Computes a power series expansion of an expression about a point to a specified order, returning a SeriesData object that carries an explicit O-term. Series handles Taylor, Laurent and Puiseux expansions, expansions at infinity, and multivariate expansions with several variable specifications. SeriesData objects can be added, multiplied, composed, differentiated and integrated with the order tracked automatically.
tools.usage:
Series[f, {x, x0, n}]
Series[f, {x, x0, n}, {y, y0, m}]
Normal[Series[...]]
tools.example:
Series[Exp[x], {x, 0, 5}]
Normal[Series[Sin[x], {x, 0, 7}]]
Series[1/(1 - x), {x, 0, 4}]
Series[Log[x], {x, 1, 3}]
Series[Exp[x] Sin[y], {x, 0, 2}, {y, 0, 2}]
tools.notes: Use Normal to drop the O-term and get an ordinary polynomial, and SeriesCoefficient to extract a single coefficient without generating the whole expansion.

tools.name: SeriesCoefficient
tools.description: Gives the coefficient of a specific power in the series expansion of a function, often as a closed-form expression in the index n. This avoids computing all lower-order terms and is the way to obtain a general formula for the coefficients of a generating function. It also accepts a SeriesData object as input.
tools.usage:
SeriesCoefficient[f, {x, x0, n}]
SeriesCoefficient[series, n]
tools.example:
SeriesCoefficient[Exp[x], {x, 0, 10}]
SeriesCoefficient[1/(1 - x - x^2), {x, 0, n}]
SeriesCoefficient[Sin[x], {x, 0, n}]
Table[SeriesCoefficient[1/(1 - 2 x), {x, 0, k}], {k, 0, 5}]
tools.notes: Generating-function coefficients often come back as piecewise or conditional expressions; use FunctionExpand or Simplify with integer assumptions to clean them up.

tools.name: Sum
tools.description: Computes finite and infinite sums symbolically, using the same iterator syntax as Table. It recognizes geometric, hypergeometric, telescoping and many special series, and can produce closed forms with symbolic limits. Multiple iterators give nested sums with the inner limits allowed to depend on outer indices.
tools.usage:
Sum[f, {i, imin, imax}]
Sum[f, {i, imin, imax, di}]
Sum[f, {i, imin, imax}, {j, jmin, jmax}]
Sum[f, {i, Infinity}]
tools.example:
Sum[i, {i, 1, n}]
Sum[1/i^2, {i, 1, Infinity}]
Sum[x^k/k!, {k, 0, Infinity}]
Sum[i j, {i, 1, 3}, {j, 1, i}]
Sum[r^k, {k, 0, Infinity}, Assumptions -> Abs[r] < 1]
tools.notes: For a purely numeric sum over a finite range, Total[Table[...]] is often faster than symbolic Sum; NSum handles slowly converging infinite sums numerically.

tools.name: NSum
tools.description: Evaluates sums numerically, including infinite sums, using extrapolation and acceleration methods rather than naive term accumulation. Options control the method, the number of terms used before extrapolation and the working precision. Use it when Sum cannot find a closed form or when the series converges too slowly for direct summation.
tools.usage:
NSum[f, {i, imin, imax}]
NSum[f, {i, imin, Infinity}]
NSum[f, {i, imin, Infinity}, Method -> m, WorkingPrecision -> p]

parameters.name: NSumTerms
parameters.description: Number of explicit terms computed before extrapolation begins.

tools.example:
NSum[1/n^2, {n, 1, Infinity}]
NSum[(-1)^n/n, {n, 1, Infinity}, Method -> "AlternatingSigns"]
NSum[1/n^1.1, {n, 1, Infinity}, WorkingPrecision -> 30]
NSum[Exp[-n^2], {n, 0, Infinity}]

tools.name: Product
tools.description: Computes finite and infinite products symbolically, using the same iterator form as Sum. It recognizes factorial, Pochhammer, Gamma and q-series patterns and can return closed forms with symbolic upper limits. Nested iterators produce multiple products.
tools.usage:
Product[f, {i, imin, imax}]
Product[f, {i, imin, imax, di}]
Product[f, {i, 1, Infinity}]
tools.example:
Product[i, {i, 1, n}]
Product[1 - 1/k^2, {k, 2, Infinity}]
Product[x + i, {i, 0, n - 1}]
Product[i j, {i, 1, 2}, {j, 1, 3}]
tools.notes: Product[i, {i, 1, n}] returns n!, and many other products come back as Pochhammer or Gamma expressions; FunctionExpand can rewrite them.

tools.name: NProduct
tools.description: Evaluates products numerically, including infinite products, using the same extrapolation machinery as NSum. It is the numeric fallback when Product cannot find a closed form. WorkingPrecision, Method and NProductFactors control accuracy and strategy.
tools.usage:
NProduct[f, {i, imin, imax}]
NProduct[f, {i, imin, Infinity}]
tools.example:
NProduct[1 - 1/k^2, {k, 2, Infinity}]
NProduct[Cos[1/n], {n, 1, Infinity}]
NProduct[1 + 1/n^2, {n, 1, Infinity}, WorkingPrecision -> 25]

tools.name: DSolve
tools.description: Solves ordinary and partial differential equations symbolically, returning a list of rules for the unknown functions. Without initial conditions the answer contains arbitrary constants C[1], C[2] or arbitrary functions; supplying conditions in the equation list produces a particular solution. Systems of equations and several unknown functions are handled by giving lists.
tools.usage:
DSolve[eqn, y[x], x]
DSolve[{eqn, y[0] == y0}, y[x], x]
DSolve[{eq1, eq2}, {y[x], z[x]}, x]
DSolve[pde, u[x, t], {x, t}]
tools.example:
DSolve[y'[x] == y[x], y[x], x]
DSolve[{y''[x] + y[x] == 0, y[0] == 1, y'[0] == 0}, y[x], x]
DSolve[y'[x] + 2 y[x] == Exp[-x], y[x], x]
DSolve[D[u[x, t], t] == D[u[x, t], x, x], u[x, t], {x, t}]
tools.notes: Write y[x] (not bare y) for the dependent variable. DSolveValue returns the expression itself instead of a rule, which avoids a ReplaceAll step.

tools.name: DSolveValue
tools.description: Solves a differential equation and returns the solution expression directly rather than a list of replacement rules. This is usually the more convenient form when there is a single expected solution, because the result can be used immediately in Plot or further calculation. It accepts exactly the same arguments and options as DSolve.
tools.usage:
DSolveValue[eqn, y[x], x]
DSolveValue[{eqn, conds}, expr, x]
tools.example:
DSolveValue[{y'[x] == -y[x], y[0] == 1}, y[x], x]
Plot[DSolveValue[{y''[t] + y[t] == 0, y[0] == 0, y'[0] == 1}, y[t], t], {t, 0, 10}]
DSolveValue[y'[x] == x y[x], y, x]
tools.notes: Requesting y rather than y[x] returns a pure Function object that can be applied at any point.

tools.name: NDSolve
tools.description: Solves ordinary and partial differential equations numerically over a specified range, returning rules mapping each unknown function to an InterpolatingFunction. It selects among stiff and non-stiff ODE methods automatically, and handles DAEs, delay equations, boundary value problems and PDEs by the method of lines. Event detection through WhenEvent allows discontinuous and hybrid systems.
tools.usage:
NDSolve[{eqns, conds}, y, {x, xmin, xmax}]
NDSolve[{eqns, conds}, {y, z}, {t, 0, T}]
NDSolve[pde, u, {x, xmin, xmax}, {t, 0, T}]

parameters.name: Method
parameters.description: Integration method, e.g. "StiffnessSwitching", "ExplicitRungeKutta", "BDF", "Adams", or a method suboption list.

parameters.name: MaxSteps
parameters.description: Maximum number of steps allowed (default 10000); raise for long integrations.

parameters.name: WorkingPrecision
parameters.description: Precision of the internal arithmetic; raise for high-accuracy solutions.

parameters.name: WhenEvent
parameters.description: Event specification inside the equation list, for discontinuities, resets or stopping conditions.

tools.notes: Ask for y rather than y[x] so the result is an InterpolatingFunction you can apply and differentiate. Use NDSolveValue when you want the function itself instead of a rule.

tools.name: NDSolveValue
tools.description: Solves a differential equation numerically and returns the InterpolatingFunction (or list of them) directly rather than replacement rules. It takes identical arguments and options to NDSolve and is the preferred form in scripts, because the result can be used immediately. The returned function reports its domain and can be differentiated and plotted.
tools.usage:
NDSolveValue[{eqns, conds}, y, {t, tmin, tmax}]
NDSolveValue[{eqns, conds}, {y, z}, {t, tmin, tmax}]

tools.name: ParametricNDSolveValue
tools.description: Creates a ParametricFunction that solves a differential equation numerically for any values of declared parameters, without re-setting up the problem each time. It is far more efficient than calling NDSolveValue inside a loop, and is the right tool for parameter sweeps, sensitivity studies and fitting ODE models to data. The result is applied like an ordinary function to the parameter values.
tools.usage: ParametricNDSolveValue[{eqns, conds}, y, {t, tmin, tmax}, {p1, p2, ...}]
tools.notes: FindFit and NonlinearModelFit can fit the parameters of a ParametricFunction to data directly.

tools.name: Residue
tools.description: Computes the residue of an expression at a pole, i.e. the coefficient of 1/(z - z0) in its Laurent expansion. It is the key ingredient for evaluating contour integrals and inverting transforms by hand. ResidueSum adds residues over all poles in a region.
tools.usage: Residue[expr, {z, z0}]
tools.example:
Residue[1/z, {z, 0}]
Residue[1/(z^2 + 1), {z, I}]
Residue[Exp[z]/z^3, {z, 0}]
2 Pi I Total[Residue[f[z], {z, #}] & /@ poles]

tools.name: Grad
tools.description: Computes the gradient of a scalar field, or the Jacobian matrix of a vector field, with respect to a list of variables. A third argument selects a coordinate system such as "Spherical" or "Cylindrical", in which case the correct metric factors are included. It is equivalent to D[f, {vars}] in Cartesian coordinates.
tools.usage:
Grad[f, {x, y, z}]
Grad[f, coords, chart]
Grad[{f1, f2}, {x, y}]
tools.example:
Grad[x^2 + y^2, {x, y}]
Grad[r^2, {r, th, ph}, "Spherical"]
Grad[{x y, y z}, {x, y, z}]
Grad[f[x, y], {x, y}]
tools.notes: The companion operators Div, Curl and Laplacian take the same coordinate-chart argument, so a whole vector calculus computation can be done in non-Cartesian coordinates.

tools.name: Div
tools.description: Computes the divergence of a vector field with respect to a list of coordinates, optionally in a named coordinate system. For a tensor field it contracts the last index. It is the standard operator for continuity and conservation equations.
tools.usage:
Div[f, {x, y, z}]
Div[f, coords, chart]
tools.example:
Div[{x, y, z}, {x, y, z}]
Div[{x^2, y^2}, {x, y}]
Div[{f[r], 0, 0}, {r, th, ph}, "Spherical"]
Simplify[Div[Grad[u[x, y], {x, y}], {x, y}]]

tools.name: Curl
tools.description: Computes the curl of a vector field in two or three dimensions, with optional coordinate-chart support. In two dimensions it returns the scalar out-of-plane component. Together with Div and Grad it completes the first-order vector differential operators.
tools.usage:
Curl[f, {x, y, z}]
Curl[f, {x, y}]
Curl[f, coords, chart]
tools.example:
Curl[{-y, x, 0}, {x, y, z}]
Curl[{-y, x}, {x, y}]
Curl[{0, 0, f[r]}, {r, th, z}, "Cylindrical"]
Simplify[Curl[Grad[f[x, y, z], {x, y, z}], {x, y, z}]]

tools.name: Laplacian
tools.description: Computes the Laplacian of a scalar or vector field, the divergence of its gradient, with optional support for curvilinear coordinate systems. In a named chart the correct metric terms appear automatically, giving for example the familiar radial form in spherical coordinates. It is the differential operator at the heart of diffusion, wave and potential equations.
tools.usage:
Laplacian[f, {x, y, z}]
Laplacian[f, coords, chart]
tools.example:
Laplacian[x^2 + y^2, {x, y}]
Laplacian[f[r], {r, th, ph}, "Spherical"]
Laplacian[u[x, y], {x, y}]
DSolve[Laplacian[u[x, y], {x, y}] == 0, u[x, y], {x, y}]

tools.name: ArcLength
tools.description: Computes the arc length of a curve given parametrically, as a graphics region, or as a geometric region object. ArcLength[{x[t], y[t]}, {t, a, b}] integrates the speed of the parametrization over the interval. It also gives the perimeter of two-dimensional regions and the length of built-in geometric primitives.
tools.usage:
ArcLength[{f1, f2, ...}, {t, a, b}]
ArcLength[curve]
ArcLength[reg]
tools.example:
ArcLength[{Cos[t], Sin[t]}, {t, 0, 2 Pi}]
ArcLength[{t, t^2}, {t, 0, 1}]
ArcLength[Circle[{0, 0}, 2]]
ArcLength[Line[{{0, 0}, {3, 4}}]]
tools.notes: Region measures Area, Volume and RegionMeasure follow the same pattern for higher-dimensional objects.

tools.name: FourierTransform
tools.description: Computes the symbolic Fourier transform of an expression with respect to a variable. The FourierParameters option selects the sign and normalization convention, which differ between mathematics, physics and signal processing traditions. It handles distributions such as DiracDelta and returns conditional results when convergence depends on parameters.
tools.usage:
FourierTransform[expr, t, w]
FourierTransform[expr, t, w, FourierParameters -> {a, b}]

parameters.name: FourierParameters
parameters.description: {a, b} selecting the convention; {0, 1} is the common signal-processing choice and {0, -2 Pi} the ordinary-frequency convention.

tools.example:
FourierTransform[Exp[-t^2], t, w]
FourierTransform[DiracDelta[t], t, w]
FourierTransform[Exp[-Abs[t]], t, w]
FourierTransform[Sin[t], t, w, FourierParameters -> {0, 1}]
tools.notes: For discrete data use Fourier; FourierSinTransform and FourierCosTransform cover the half-line transforms.

tools.name: InverseFourierTransform
tools.description: Computes the symbolic inverse Fourier transform, recovering a function of t from its transform in w. It accepts the same FourierParameters convention option, which must match the one used for the forward transform. Combined with FourierTransform it solves linear differential and convolution equations.
tools.usage:
InverseFourierTransform[expr, w, t]
InverseFourierTransform[expr, w, t, FourierParameters -> {a, b}]
tools.example:
InverseFourierTransform[Sqrt[Pi] Exp[-w^2/4], w, t]
InverseFourierTransform[1/(1 + w^2), w, t]
InverseFourierTransform[FourierTransform[f[t], t, w], w, t]

tools.name: LaplaceTransform
tools.description: Computes the one-sided Laplace transform of an expression from the time variable to the transform variable s. It knows the derivative rule, so transforming a differential equation converts it into an algebraic equation in s with the initial values appearing explicitly. Results may be ConditionalExpression objects giving the region of convergence.
tools.usage:
LaplaceTransform[expr, t, s]
LaplaceTransform[expr, t, s, Assumptions -> assum]
tools.example:
LaplaceTransform[Exp[-a t], t, s]
LaplaceTransform[t^2, t, s]
LaplaceTransform[Sin[w t], t, s]
LaplaceTransform[y''[t], t, s]
tools.notes: The standard workflow is LaplaceTransform the ODE, Solve for the transform of the unknown, then InverseLaplaceTransform back.

tools.name: InverseLaplaceTransform
tools.description: Computes the inverse Laplace transform, recovering a function of t from an expression in s. It handles rational functions by partial fractions and many transcendental transforms by table lookup and contour methods. Use Apart first when a rational transform does not invert directly.
tools.usage: InverseLaplaceTransform[expr, s, t]
tools.example:
InverseLaplaceTransform[1/(s + a), s, t]
InverseLaplaceTransform[1/(s^2 + w^2), s, t]
InverseLaplaceTransform[Apart[(s + 3)/(s^2 + 3 s + 2)], s, t]
InverseLaplaceTransform[Exp[-s]/s, s, t]

tools.name: ZTransform
tools.description: Computes the Z transform of a sequence expression in a discrete index n, giving a function of z. It is the discrete-time analogue of the Laplace transform and converts linear difference equations into algebraic ones. InverseZTransform recovers the sequence.
tools.usage:
ZTransform[expr, n, z]
InverseZTransform[expr, z, n]
tools.example:
ZTransform[a^n, n, z]
ZTransform[n, n, z]
ZTransform[Sin[w n], n, z]
InverseZTransform[z/(z - a), z, n]
tools.notes: Results often carry convergence conditions such as Abs[z] > Abs[a]; supply Assumptions to get an unconditional answer.

tools.name: InverseZTransform
tools.description: Computes the inverse Z transform, recovering a sequence in the index n from a function of z. Rational transforms are inverted through partial fractions, giving geometric and polynomial-times-geometric terms. It is the final step when solving a linear difference equation with the Z transform.
tools.usage: InverseZTransform[expr, z, n]
tools.example:
InverseZTransform[z/(z - 2), z, n]
InverseZTransform[1/(z - 1)^2, z, n]
InverseZTransform[ZTransform[f[n], n, z], z, n]

tools.name: FourierSeries
tools.description: Gives the n-th order exponential Fourier series approximation of a function on the interval -Pi to Pi (scaled by the FourierParameters option). FourierTrigSeries gives the equivalent sine/cosine form, and FourierCoefficient extracts a single coefficient. These are symbolic tools for periodic expansions, distinct from the discrete Fourier transform.
tools.usage:
FourierSeries[expr, t, n]
FourierTrigSeries[expr, t, n]
FourierCoefficient[expr, t, k]
tools.example:
FourierSeries[t, t, 3]
FourierTrigSeries[Abs[t], t, 4]
FourierCoefficient[t^2, t, 1]
Plot[Evaluate[FourierTrigSeries[UnitStep[t], t, 5]], {t, -Pi, Pi}]

tools.name: Convolve
tools.description: Computes the symbolic convolution integral of two functions with respect to a variable, producing a function of the output variable. It is the continuous counterpart of ListConvolve and the operation that multiplication of Fourier or Laplace transforms corresponds to. DiscreteConvolve handles sequences indexed by integers.
tools.usage:
Convolve[f, g, x, y]
DiscreteConvolve[f, g, n, m]
tools.example:
Convolve[Exp[-x] UnitStep[x], UnitStep[x], x, y]
Convolve[UnitBox[x], UnitBox[x], x, y]
DiscreteConvolve[a^n, UnitStep[n], n, m]
tools.notes: Convolution of two functions supported on the half-line corresponds to multiplying their Laplace transforms, which is often a faster route to the answer.

tools.name: Asymptotic
tools.description: Computes asymptotic approximations of expressions, sums, integrals and equation solutions as a variable approaches a limit point. AsymptoticExpansion gives a series expansion valid asymptotically, while related functions cover integrals (AsymptoticIntegrate), sums (AsymptoticSum), differential equations (AsymptoticDSolveValue) and equation roots (AsymptoticSolve). They handle cases where an ordinary Series expansion does not exist.
tools.usage:
Asymptotic[expr, x -> x0]
Asymptotic[expr, {x, x0, n}]
AsymptoticIntegrate[f, {x, a, b}, eps -> 0]
AsymptoticDSolveValue[eqn, y, x, eps -> 0]
tools.example:
Asymptotic[Gamma[x], x -> Infinity]
Asymptotic[Log[1 + x]/x, {x, 0, 3}]
AsymptoticIntegrate[Exp[-x/eps], {x, 0, 1}, {eps, 0, 2}]
AsymptoticSolve[x^2 + eps x - 1 == 0, x, {eps, 0, 2}]
tools.notes: Asymptotic expansions are generally divergent series that approximate well for large arguments; do not treat them as convergent.

tools.name: DiscreteLimit
tools.description: Computes the limit of a sequence as the integer index tends to infinity, using methods appropriate to discrete rather than continuous variables. It handles sequences defined by factorials, binomials and other integer-only expressions where the continuous Limit would be incorrect or undefined. DiscreteMaxLimit and DiscreteMinLimit give the limit superior and inferior.
tools.usage:
DiscreteLimit[f, n -> Infinity]
DiscreteMaxLimit[f, n -> Infinity]
tools.example:
DiscreteLimit[(1 + 1/n)^n, n -> Infinity]
DiscreteLimit[n!/n^n, n -> Infinity]
DiscreteLimit[(-1)^n, n -> Infinity]
DiscreteMaxLimit[Sin[n], n -> Infinity]

tools.name: DifferenceDelta
tools.description: Computes the forward difference of an expression with respect to a discrete variable, the discrete analogue of D. DifferenceDelta[f, {n, k}] applies the operator k times and a step size can be specified. It is used to set up and analyze difference equations and discrete sums.
tools.usage:
DifferenceDelta[f, n]
DifferenceDelta[f, {n, k}]
DifferenceDelta[f, {n, k, h}]
tools.example:
DifferenceDelta[n^2, n]
DifferenceDelta[a^n, n]
DifferenceDelta[n^3, {n, 2}]
Sum[DifferenceDelta[f[k], k], {k, 1, n}]
tools.notes: DiscreteShift shifts the index directly, and SumConvergence tests convergence of the corresponding series.

tools.name: RSolve
tools.description: Solves recurrence and functional equations symbolically, returning closed-form expressions for the sequence. With initial conditions supplied it gives a particular solution; otherwise arbitrary constants C[1], C[2] appear. It handles linear recurrences with constant or polynomial coefficients, systems of recurrences and some nonlinear cases.
tools.usage:
RSolve[eqn, a[n], n]
RSolve[{eqn, a[0] == a0}, a[n], n]
RSolve[{eq1, eq2}, {a[n], b[n]}, n]
RSolveValue[eqn, a[n], n]
tools.example:
RSolve[a[n] == a[n - 1] + a[n - 2], a[n], n]
RSolve[{a[n] == 2 a[n - 1], a[1] == 3}, a[n], n]
RSolveValue[{f[n] == n f[n - 1], f[0] == 1}, f[n], n]
RSolve[a[n + 1] == a[n]/(1 + a[n]), a[n], n]
tools.notes: RecurrenceTable generates numeric values from a recurrence when no closed form is needed or available, and is much faster for long sequences.

tools.name: RecurrenceTable
tools.description: Generates a table of values satisfying a recurrence equation with given initial conditions, iterating numerically or exactly without seeking a closed form. It uses the same iterator specification as Table for the index range. This is the efficient way to produce long sequences from a recurrence.
tools.usage:
RecurrenceTable[{eqns, inits}, a, {n, nmin, nmax}]
RecurrenceTable[{eqns, inits}, {a, b}, {n, nmin, nmax}]
tools.example:
RecurrenceTable[{a[n] == a[n - 1] + a[n - 2], a[1] == 1, a[2] == 1}, a, {n, 1, 20}]
RecurrenceTable[{x[n + 1] == 3.9 x[n] (1 - x[n]), x[0] == 0.2}, x, {n, 0, 100}]
ListPlot[RecurrenceTable[{a[n] == a[n - 1]/2 + 1, a[0] == 10}, a, {n, 0, 20}]]
tools.notes: For a linear recurrence with constant coefficients, LinearRecurrence is even faster and takes the coefficient list directly.
